#### Remark 7.9 (Weyl is a barrier).

If $H$ were smaller than $T^{\frac{1}{3}}$ , then $\RHS\eqref{eqn:t_principal_contribution}=T^{\frac{3}{2}}H^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ would be bigger than $TH$ , and (7.57) would be weaker than Lindelöf on average. Therefore, to get a sub-Weyl bound by our method, we would need to obtain cancellation in $\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_principal_contribution}$ . This is exactly as predicted in Section 4. Indeed, by Proposition 7.8, $\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_principal_contribution}$ is essentially a sum over $t_{r}\lesssim T/H$ , and if we approximate this sum by the top dyadic range, then

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_principal_contribution}\approx\Big|\sum_{t_{r}\sim T/H}{\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=10.83334pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle W$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=10.83334pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle W$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.40926pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.40926pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.78334pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=8.59724pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle W$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.9537pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.9537pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.41667pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=7.264pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle W$}\crcr}}}}}(s_{r})\widetilde{C}_{r}^{2}\Big|=E_{\textnormal{true}}, $$

where the last equality uses the notation (4) from Section 4. It seems difficult to prove a nontrivial bound for this sum (without using the crossing equation which would put us back where we started). One reason is that ${\mathchoice{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=10.83334pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\displaystyle W$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 7.09259pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 7.09259pt\hbox{$\textstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=6.83331pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=10.83334pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\textstyle W$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 6.40926pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 6.40926pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=4.78334pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=8.59724pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptstyle W$}\crcr}}}}{{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hbox{\raise 5.9537pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}[-1]{\lower 5.9537pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\widehat{\vrule width=0.0pt,height=3.41667pt\vrule height=0.0pt,width=7.264pt}$}}}}\cr\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle W$}\crcr}}}}}(\tfrac{1}{2}+it)$ oscillates quickly for $t\sim T/H$ . Specifically, by (7.8) in Proposition 7.8, it oscillates at frequency $\alpha^{\prime}(t)\sim\log T$ , where $\alpha(t)$ is as in (7.22). For comparison, the cutoff $\mathds{1}_{|t-T|\lesssim T^{\frac{1}{3}}}$ oscillates at frequency $\sim T^{-\frac{1}{3}}$ , far less than $\log T$ . However, it already tests the limits of our abilities to sum this cutoff against $\widetilde{C}_{r}^{2}$ . Another sign that the frequency $\log T$ is too fast to handle is that the distribution of the spectral parameters $t_{r}$ is not known at the dual scale $\frac{1}{\log T}$ . For example, it is conjectured but not known that, for every $c>0$ and $T\gg_{c}1$ , there exists $r$ with $t_{r}\in[T,T+\frac{c}{\log T}]$ . When $c$ is a sufficiently large constant, this is true by [51] (in constant negative curvature) or [2] (in variable negative curvature).

## 8. Trivial bounds for conformal blocks when $t\leq 1$

Let $s\in(\frac{1}{2},1]\cup(\frac{1}{2}+i\mathbf{R}_{\geq 0})$ . Write $s=\sigma+it$ . The next two propositions are proved in Subsections 8.1 and 8.2, respectively.

#### Proposition 8.1 (Trivial bound for u-channel conformal block when $t\leq 1$ ).

Assume $t\leq 1$ . Let $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $\re z>0$ and $|z|\ll 1$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle|H_{s}(1-z^{2})|\lesssim\log(|z|^{-1}). $$

#### Proposition 8.2 (Trivial bound for t-channel conformal block when $t\leq 1$ ).

Assume $t\leq 1$ . Let $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $\re z>0$ and $|z|\ll 1$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle|H_{s}(1-z^{-2})|\lesssim|z|^{2(1-\sigma)}\log(|z|^{-1})\leq\log(|z|^{-1}). $$

Assume in the remainder of this section that $t\leq 1$ . This assumption will often be used to estimate $|\zeta^{s}|\sim|\zeta|^{\sigma}$ for $\zeta\in\mathbf{C}\setminus(-\infty,0]$ .

### 8.1. u-Channel

Here we prove Proposition 8.1. This is trivial when $s=1$ because $H_{0}$ is identically $1$ , so we may assume $\sigma<1$ . Then by Euler’s integral representation [36, (9.1.6)] for the hypergeometric ${}_{2}F_{1}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle H_{s}(1-z^{2})={}_{2}F_{1}(1-s,s;1;1-z^{2})=\frac{1}{\Gamma(s)\Gamma(1-s)}\int_{0}^{1}x^{s-1}(1-x)^{-s}(1-x(1-z^{2}))^{s-1}\,dx. $$

Replacing $x$ with $1-x$ and using Euler’s reflection formula for the Gamma function,

$$ \displaystyle H_{s}(1-z^{2})=\frac{\sin(\pi s)}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}(1-x)^{s-1}x^{-s}(x+z^{2}(1-x))^{s-1}\,dx. $$

Let $I(x)$ denote the integrand, so

$$ \displaystyle I(x)=(1-x)^{s-1}x^{-s}(x+z^{2}(1-x))^{s-1}. $$

Bearing in mind that $|z|\ll 1$ , we trivially have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}|I(x)|\,dx\lesssim\int_{0}^{1}(1-x)^{\sigma-1}\,dx\lesssim 1, $$

where the second inequality is because $1-\sigma\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . Write $z=re^{i\theta}$ in polar coordinates. Then

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}|I(x)|\,dx\lesssim\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}x^{-\sigma}|x+r^{2}e^{2i\theta}(1-x)|^{\sigma-1}\,dx. $$

Making the substitution $x=r^{2}y$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}|I(x)|\,dx \displaystyle\lesssim r^{2}\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}r^{-2}}(r^{2}y)^{-\sigma}|r^{2}y+r^{2}e^{2i\theta}(1-r^{2}y)|^{\sigma-1}\,dy \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}r^{-2}}y^{-\sigma}|y+e^{2i\theta}(1-r^{2}y)|^{\sigma-1}\,dy. $$

Rearranging the expression in absolute values,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}|I(x)|\,dx\lesssim\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}r^{-2}}y^{-\sigma}|e^{2i\theta}+(1-r^{2}e^{2i\theta})y|^{\sigma-1}\,dy. $$

Since $r\ll 1$ , the absolute value on the right is $\gtrsim 1$ when $y\leq\frac{1}{2}$ and $\gtrsim y$ when $y\geq 2$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}|I(x)|\,dx \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}y^{-\sigma}\,dy+\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2}|e^{2i\theta}+(1-r^{2}e^{2i\theta})y|^{\sigma-1}\,dy+\int_{2}^{\frac{1}{2}r^{-2}}y^{-1}\,dy \displaystyle\lesssim\frac{1}{1-\sigma}+\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{2}|e^{2i\theta}+(1-r^{2}e^{2i\theta})y|^{\sigma-1}\,dy+\log(r^{-1}). $$

Using the inequality $|\zeta|\geq|\re\zeta|$ and then making the substitution $u=(1-r^{2}\cos(2\theta))y$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}|I(x)|\,dx\lesssim\frac{1}{1-\sigma}+\log(r^{-1})+\int_{u\sim 1}|\cos(2\theta)+u|^{\sigma-1}\,du. $$

The integral on the right hand side is $\lesssim 1$ because $1-\sigma\leq\frac{1}{2}$ , so

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}|I(x)|\,dx\lesssim\frac{1}{1-\sigma}+\log(r^{-1}). $$

Inserting (8.4) and (8.5) into (8.3),

$$ \displaystyle|H_{s}(1-z^{2})|\lesssim\frac{|\sin(\pi s)|}{1-\sigma}+|\sin(\pi s)|\log(r^{-1}). $$

In the range of $s$ that we are considering, we have $|\sin(\pi s)|\lesssim 1-\sigma\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle|H_{s}(1-z^{2})|\lesssim\log(r^{-1}). $$

This is the desired bound (8.1). ∎

### 8.2. t-Channel

The proof of Proposition 8.2 is closely analogous to that of Proposition 8.1. Again, the result is trivial when $s=1$ , so assume $\sigma<1$ . Then Euler’s integral representation [36, (9.1.6)] gives

$$ \displaystyle H_{s}(1-z^{-2})={}_{2}F_{1}(1-s;s;1;1-z^{-2})=\frac{1}{\Gamma(s)\Gamma(1-s)}\int_{0}^{1}x^{s-1}(1-x)^{-s}(1-x(1-z^{-2}))^{s-1}\,dx. $$

Pulling a factor of $z^{2(1-s)}$ out of the integrand and using Euler’s reflection formula,

$$ \displaystyle H_{s}(1-z^{-2})=z^{2(1-s)}\frac{\sin(\pi s)}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}x^{s-1}(1-x)^{-s}(x+z^{2}(1-x))^{s-1}\,dx. $$

The only differences between this and (8.3) are the factor of $z^{2(1-s)}$ in front and the fact that $x$ and $1-x$ have switched places in the first two factors in the integrand. Estimating the integral in the same way as (8.3) yields

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\frac{\sin(\pi s)}{\pi}\int_{0}^{1}x^{s-1}(1-x)^{-s}(x+z^{2}(1-x))^{s-1}\,dx\Big|\lesssim\log(|z|^{-1}), $$

from which the desired bound (8.2) follows. ∎

## 9. Asymptotics for conformal blocks when $t>1$

Suppose $r\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ is such that $t_{r}>1$ (or more generally $t_{r}>0$ ). Then $\sigma_{r}=\frac{1}{2}$ , so $t_{r}$ determines $s_{r}=\frac{1}{2}+it_{r}$ . Therefore, in this section, the variable $t$ should be thought of as a spectral parameter, and we free the variables $s$ and $\sigma$ so that they have no special meaning.

The two propositions below are the most precise asymptotics for the u- and t-channel conformal blocks that we will use. They are proven in Subsections 9.1 and 9.2, respectively. Along the way, we will establish some more crude but useful estimates.

#### Proposition 9.1 (Asymptotic for u-channel conformal block when $t>1$ ).

There exist constants $c_{j}\in\mathbf{Q}$ with $c_{0}=1$ , such that the following holds. Let $t>1$ . Let $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $t^{-1}\lesssim|z|\lesssim 1$ and $\re z\gtrsim t^{-\frac{2}{3}+\varepsilon}|z|$ . Then for each $M\geq 0$ , there exists $J\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ depending only on $M$ and $\varepsilon$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\frac{t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}}{2\sqrt{\pi z}}\Big[e^{-2tz}\sum_{j=0}^{J}c_{j}(tz^{3})^{j}+O_{M}(e^{-2t\re z}|tz|^{-1}+t^{-M})\Big]. $$

Recall that implicit constants are allowed to depend on $\varepsilon$ . Inspecting the proof of Proposition 9.1 shows that one can take

$$ \displaystyle c_{j}=\frac{(-1)^{j}}{3^{j}(j!)}. $$

At first, it may seem odd that (9.1) is an asymptotic expansion in powers of $tz^{3}$ , but that we never assume $tz^{3}$ is small. However, if $|tz^{3}|\gtrsim 1$ , then the hypothesis $\re z\gtrsim t^{-\frac{2}{3}+\varepsilon}|z|$ forces

$$ \displaystyle\re tz\gtrsim t^{\frac{1}{3}+\varepsilon}|z|=t^{\varepsilon}|tz^{3}|^{\frac{1}{3}}\gtrsim t^{\varepsilon}, $$

and so the exponential decay of the factor $e^{-2tz}$ dominates the polynomial growth of the sum on the right hand side of (9.1).

#### Proposition 9.2 (Asymptotic for t-channel conformal block when $t>1$ ).

Let $t>1$ . Let $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $\re z>0$ , $\im z\geq 0$ , and $|z|\ll 1$ . Denote

$$ \displaystyle\phi(z)=-\log(1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\psi(z)=\frac{\pi^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-i\pi/4}}{1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}}}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})=t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}z\psi(z)e^{-2it[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)]}(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{4}))+O(t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}|z|e^{-\pi t}). $$

Assume in the remainder of this section that $t>1$ . Then by the definition (3.23),

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}=t^{4k-2}\,e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}. $$

### 9.1. u-Channel

Let $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $\re z>0$ . Our starting point is Barnes’s contour integral representation [47, (15.6.7)], which gives

$$ \displaystyle H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\frac{1}{2\pi i\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}+it)^{2}\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}-it)^{2}}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}\Gamma(s)^{2}\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it-s\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it-s\Big)z^{-2s}\,ds $$

for any $\sigma\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . For a proof of this integral representation, see [61, Section 14.53]. By Euler’s reflection formula,

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it\Big)=\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi(\frac{1}{2}+it))}=\frac{2\pi}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}. $$

Therefore, multiplying both sides of (9.3) by $\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}+it)^{2}\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}-it)^{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Big(\frac{2\pi}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Big)^{2}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}\Gamma(s)^{2}\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it-s\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it-s\Big)z^{-2s}\,ds. $$

The next lemma gives an upper bound for the integrand.

#### Lemma 9.3.

Let $\sigma\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . Let $s\in\mathbf{C}$ with $\re s=\sigma$ . Let $\delta\in[0,1]$ be such that $\re z\geq\delta|z|$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\Gamma(s)^{2}\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it-s\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it-s\Big)z^{-2s}\Big|\lesssim_{\sigma}e^{-\pi t}|z|^{-2\sigma}|s|^{2\sigma-1}e^{-2\delta|s|}. $$

#### Proof.

Write $z=re^{i\theta}$ with $|\theta|<\frac{\pi}{2}$ . For any $\sigma_{0}>0$ , on the vertical strip $\sigma_{0}\leq\re w\leq 1$ , the Gamma function is bounded by

$$ \displaystyle|\Gamma(w)|\lesssim_{\sigma_{0}}|w|^{\re w-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}|w|}. $$

Therefore the left hand side of (9.5) satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:contour_integrand_bd}\lesssim_{\sigma}|s|^{2\sigma-1}e^{-\pi|s|}|s-it|^{-\sigma}|s+it|^{-\sigma}e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}(|s-it|+|s+it|)}r^{-2\sigma}e^{2\theta\im s}. $$

Crudely estimate

$$ \displaystyle|s\pm it|^{-\sigma}\lesssim_{\sigma}1 $$

and

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}(|s-it|+|s+it|)}\leq e^{-\pi t} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\pi|s|}e^{2\theta\im s}\lesssim e^{-(\pi-2|\theta|)|s|}. $$

Putting these estimates together,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:contour_integrand_bd}\lesssim_{\sigma}e^{-\pi t}r^{-2\sigma}|s|^{2\sigma-1}e^{-(\pi-2|\theta|)|s|}. $$

Observe that

$$ \displaystyle\pi-2|\theta|=2(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-|\theta|)\geq 2\sin(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-|\theta|)=2\cos\theta\geq 2\delta. $$

Inserting this into (9.6) yields (9.5). ∎

Trivially estimating the right hand side of (9.4) using Lemma 9.3 gives

#### Proposition 9.4.

Assume $|z|\geq T^{-O(1)}$ and $\re z\geq T^{-O(1)}|z|$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})|\lessapprox t^{4k-2}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\sigma\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . Combining (9.4) with Lemma 9.3,

$$ \displaystyle\Big(\frac{2\pi}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Big)^{2}|H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})|\lesssim_{\sigma}e^{-\pi t}|z|^{-2\sigma}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}|s|^{2\sigma-1}e^{-T^{-O(1)}|s|}|ds|. $$

Writing $|z|^{-2\sigma}\leq T^{O(\sigma)}$ and multiplying both sides by $e^{\pi t}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\pi t}|H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})|\lesssim_{\sigma}T^{O(\sigma)}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}|s|^{2\sigma-1}e^{-T^{-O(1)}|s|}|ds|. $$

The exponential factor in the integrand is essentially a cutoff to $|s|\lesssim T^{O(1)}$ , so

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\pi t}|H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})|\lesssim_{\sigma}T^{O(\sigma)}\int_{\begin{subarray}{c}\re s=\sigma\\
|s|\lesssim T^{O(1)}\end{subarray}}|s|^{2\sigma-1}|ds|\lesssim_{\sigma}T^{O(\sigma)}. $$

Since this holds for arbitrary $\sigma>0$ , we deduce

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\pi t}|H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})|\lessapprox 1. $$

This is equivalent to (9.7). ∎

We now turn to the main result of this subsection, Proposition 9.1.

#### Proof of Proposition 9.1.

Let $z$ be as in Proposition 9.1, so $t^{-1}\lesssim|z|\lesssim 1$ and $\re z\gtrsim t^{-\frac{2}{3}+\varepsilon}|z|$ . Fix $\sigma\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ , say $\sigma=\frac{1}{4}$ for concreteness. Then by (9.4), together with Lemma 9.3 to bound the tails in (9.4),

$$ \displaystyle\Big(\frac{2\pi}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Big)^{2}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\begin{subarray}{c}\re s=\sigma\\
|s|\leq t^{\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}\end{subarray}}\Gamma(s)^{2}\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it-s\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it-s\Big)z^{-2s}\,ds+O(e^{-\pi t}t^{-\infty}). $$

Stirling’s approximation says that for $w\in\mathbf{C}$ with, say, $\re w\geq-0.49$ and $|\im w|\gtrsim 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\log\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}+w\Big)=w\log w-w+\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi)+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{a_{n}}{w^{2n+1}}+O(|w|^{-\infty}) $$

for some constants $a_{n}\in\mathbf{Q}$ . This infinite series is generally divergent, so it should be interpreted in the usual asymptotic sense, namely that for any $M\geq 0$ , there exists $N\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ such that if the series is replaced by the $N$ th partial sum, then the error is $O_{M}(|w|^{-M})$ . Since the domain of integration in (9.8) is truncated to $|s|\leq t^{\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}$ , we have $|\im(\pm it-s)|\sim t$ . Thus by Stirling,

$$ \displaystyle\log\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}\pm it-s\Big)=(\pm it-s)\log(\pm it-s)-(\pm it-s)+\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi)+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{a_{n}}{(\pm it-s)^{2n+1}}+O(t^{-\infty}). $$

Summing this asymptotic for $\log\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}+it-s)$ and $\log\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}-it-s)$ , and then writing $\pm it-s=\pm it(1+\pm i\frac{s}{t})$ and expanding in powers of $s/t=O(t^{-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\log\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it-s\Big)+\log\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it-s\Big)=-\pi t-2s\log t+\log(2\pi)+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell=0}^{j}b_{j,\ell}\frac{s^{2\ell+1}}{t^{2j}}+O(t^{-\infty}) $$

for some constants $b_{j,\ell}\in\mathbf{Q}$ . Exponentiating,

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it-s\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it-s\Big)=2\pi e^{-\pi t}t^{-2s}\exp\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell=0}^{j}b_{j,\ell}\frac{s^{2\ell+1}}{t^{2j}}+O(t^{-\infty})\Big). $$

Since $|s|\leq t^{\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}$ , each term in the series is $O(t^{-\frac{3}{2}\varepsilon})$ (indeed, the asymptotically largest term is $s^{3}/t^{2}=O(t^{-\frac{3}{2}\varepsilon})$ , corresponding to $j=\ell=1$ ). In addition, since the series is interpreted in the asymptotic sense, we are only interested in finitely many terms at a time. We can therefore Taylor expand the exponential, to get

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it-s\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it-s\Big)=2\pi e^{-\pi t}t^{-2s}(1+O(t^{-\infty}))\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell=0}^{3j}c_{j,\ell}\frac{s^{\ell}}{t^{2j}} $$

for some constants $c_{j,\ell}\in\mathbf{Q}$ with $c_{0,0}=1$ . Inserting this into (9.8),

$$ \displaystyle\Big(\frac{2\pi}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Big)^{2}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2}) \displaystyle=\frac{e^{-\pi t}}{i}\int_{\begin{subarray}{c}\re s=\sigma\\
|s|\leq t^{\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}\end{subarray}}\Gamma(s)^{2}(tz)^{-2s}(1+O(t^{-\infty}))\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell=0}^{3j}c_{j,\ell}\frac{s^{\ell}}{t^{2j}}\,ds \displaystyle+O(e^{-\pi t}t^{-\infty}). $$

Rearranging factors of $2$ , $\pi$ , and $e^{\pi t}$ , and using that $e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}=e^{\pi t}(1+O(t^{-\infty}))$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\pi e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\frac{1}{4\pi i}\int_{\begin{subarray}{c}\re s=\sigma\\
|s|\leq t^{\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}\end{subarray}}\Gamma(s)^{2}(tz)^{-2s}(1+O(t^{-\infty}))\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\sum_{\ell=0}^{3j}c_{j,\ell}\frac{s^{\ell}}{t^{2j}}\,ds+O(t^{-\infty}). $$

Switching the sums and the integral (which is valid because the sums are interpreted in the asymptotic sense and hence are really finite sums), and absorbing the error term in the integral into the error term outside the integral,

$$ \displaystyle\pi e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}t^{-2j}\sum_{\ell=0}^{3j}\frac{c_{j,\ell}}{4\pi i}\int_{\begin{subarray}{c}\re s=\sigma\\
|s|\leq t^{\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}\end{subarray}}\Gamma(s)^{2}(tz)^{-2s}s^{\ell}\,ds+O(t^{-\infty}). $$

By a similar computation to Lemma 9.3, the integrand decays exponentially once $|s|$ exceeds $t^{\frac{2}{3}-\varepsilon}$ , so in particular the integrand is $\lesssim|s|^{-\infty}$ for $|s|>t^{\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}}$ . Thus we can complete the integral:

$$ \displaystyle\pi e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}t^{-2j}\sum_{\ell=0}^{3j}\frac{c_{j,\ell}}{4\pi i}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}\Gamma(s)^{2}(tz)^{-2s}s^{\ell}\,ds+O(t^{-\infty}). $$

Rewrite this as

$$ \displaystyle\pi e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}t^{-2j}\sum_{\ell=0}^{3j}\frac{d_{j,\ell}}{4\pi i}(z\partial_{z})^{\ell}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}\Gamma(s)^{2}(tz)^{-2s}\,ds+O(t^{-\infty}), $$

with $d_{j,\ell}=(-1)^{\ell}2^{-\ell}c_{j,\ell}$ . So $d_{j,\ell}\in\mathbf{Q}$ and $d_{0,0}=1$ . Using the integral representation

$$ \displaystyle K_{0}(w)=\frac{1}{4\pi i}\int_{\sigma-i\infty}^{\sigma+i\infty}\Gamma(s)^{2}(w/2)^{-2s}\,ds $$

for the Bessel function $K_{0}$ [47, (10.32.13)], the above simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\pi e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}t^{-2j}\sum_{\ell=0}^{3j}d_{j,\ell}(z\partial_{z})^{\ell}[K_{0}(2tz)]+O(t^{-\infty}). $$

Expanding $(z\partial_{z})^{\ell}$ using the product rule shows that $(z\partial_{z})^{\ell}$ is a $\mathbf{Z}$ -linear combination of $\{z^{m}\partial_{z}^{m}\}_{0\leq m\leq\ell}$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\pi e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}t^{-2j}\sum_{m=0}^{3j}e_{j,m}(tz)^{m}K_{0}^{(m)}(2tz)+O(t^{-\infty}) $$

for some constants $e_{j,m}\in\mathbf{Q}$ with $e_{0,0}=1$ . By [36, (5.6.9)], the $m$ th derivative $K_{0}^{(m)}$ is $(-1)^{m}$ times a finite convex combination of $\{K_{\nu}\}_{\nu\in\mathbf{Z}}$ . By [36, (5.11.9)], for $w\in\mathbf{C}\setminus(-\infty,0]$ with $|w|\gtrsim 1$ and $|\Arg w|\leq\pi-\delta$ for some $\delta>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle K_{\nu}(w)=e^{-w}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2w}}\,(1+O_{\nu,\delta}(|w|^{-1})). $$

It follows that for $w$ satisfying the same conditions,

$$ \displaystyle K_{0}^{(m)}(w)=(-1)^{m}e^{-w}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2w}}\,(1+O_{m,\delta}(|w|^{-1})). $$

By assumption, $|z|\gtrsim t^{-1}$ , and so $|tz|\gtrsim 1$ . In addition, by assumption, $\re z>0$ . Thus we can apply the above asymptotic for $K_{0}^{(m)}$ to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\pi e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2}) \displaystyle=e^{-2tz}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{4tz}}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}t^{-2j}\sum_{m=0}^{3j}f_{j,m}(tz)^{m}(1+O_{m}(|tz|^{-1}))+O(t^{-\infty}) \displaystyle=e^{-2tz}\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{tz}}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}f_{j,3j}t^{-2j}(tz)^{3j}(1+O_{j}(|tz|^{-1}))+O(t^{-\infty}) $$

with $f_{j,m}=(-1)^{m}e_{j,m}$ . Again, $f_{j,m}\in\mathbf{Q}$ and $f_{0,0}=1$ . Denote $c_{j}=f_{j,3j}$ , so $c_{j}\in\mathbf{Q}$ with $c_{0}=1$ . Then multiplying both sides above by $\frac{1}{\pi}t^{4k-2}$ , and simplifying,

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\frac{t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}}{2\sqrt{\pi z}}\Big[e^{-2tz}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}c_{j}(tz^{3})^{j}(1+O_{j}(|tz|^{-1}))\Big]+O(t^{-\infty}). $$

We claim that we can rewrite the right hand side to get

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=\frac{t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}}{2\sqrt{\pi z}}\Big[e^{-2tz}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}c_{j}(tz^{3})^{j}+O(e^{-2t\re z}|tz|^{-1}+t^{-\infty})\Big]. $$

If $|tz^{3}|\lesssim 1$ , then this is clear. If $|tz^{3}|\gtrsim 1$ , then as mentioned above, our assumption $\re z\gtrsim t^{-\frac{2}{3}+\varepsilon}|z|$ implies the lower bound

$$ \displaystyle\re(tz)\gtrsim t^{\frac{1}{3}+\varepsilon}|z|=t^{\varepsilon}|tz^{3}|^{\frac{1}{3}}\gtrsim t^{\varepsilon}, $$

and hence the exponential factor on the right hand side of (9.10) is extremely small and dominates the rest of the asymptotic. In particular, $\RHS\eqref{eqn:u_asymptotic_before_claim}\lesssim t^{-\infty}$ . Thus (9.11) holds in this case as well. In summary, we have proved (9.11) both when $|tz^{3}|\lesssim 1$ and when $|tz^{3}|\gtrsim 1$ , so (9.11) holds in general. Since (9.11) is interpreted in the asymptotic sense, the content of (9.11) is precisely Proposition 9.1. This concludes the proof. ∎

#### Corollary 9.5.

Assume $t\geq T\log^{2}T$ . Let $z$ be as in (5.14). Then

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})|\lesssim t^{-\infty}. $$

#### Proof.

Note that $z$ obeys the assumptions of Proposition 9.1. Therefore, we can take absolute values in (9.1) to get

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})|\lesssim_{M}t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}|z|^{-\frac{1}{2}}[e^{-2t/T}t^{O_{M}(1)}+t^{-M}] $$

for any $M$ . Since $|z|\geq T^{-1}$ and $t\geq T\log^{2}T$ , we have $|z|^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-2t/T}\lesssim t^{-\infty}$ . We conclude (9.12). ∎

A corollary of (9.9) in the proof of Proposition 9.1 is

#### Corollary 9.6.

Assume $t\gg 1$ . Assume also that $z$ is real and positive, and that $z\sim t^{-1}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle 0\leq\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})\sim t^{4k-2}. $$

#### Proof.

As explained in the proof of Proposition 7.2, $\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})$ is nonnegative because $\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}$ has nonnegative Taylor coefficients at the origin.

Now, the assumptions on $z$ in Corollary 9.6 imply the assumptions on $z$ in Proposition 9.1, so (9.9) is valid. Since $tz\sim 1$ , the sum over $m$ in (9.9) is $O_{j}(1)$ . Therefore, retaining only the $j=0$ term in (9.9),

$$ \displaystyle\pi e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})=K_{0}(2tz)+O(t^{-2}). $$

The $K_{0}$ Bessel function is positive and of size $\sim 1$ on $\{x\sim 1\}$ . Since $t\gg 1$ , it follows that

$$ \displaystyle e^{-\pi t}H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{2})\sim 1. $$

This is equivalent to (9.13). ∎

### 9.2. t-Channel

We only need one simple lemma before beginning the proof of Proposition 9.2.

#### Lemma 9.7.

Let $h$ be a holomorphic function defined on a neighborhood of the origin. Assume $h$ is real-valued on the real line. Let $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $|z|\ll_{h}1$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle|\im h(z)|\lesssim_{h}|\im z|. $$

#### Proof.

Let $z=x+iy$ . Since $h$ is real-valued on the real line, $\im h(x)=0$ . Thus we can write

$$ \displaystyle|\im h(z)|=|\im(h(z)-h(x))|\leq|h(z)-h(x)|=\Big|\int_{0}^{y}h^{\prime}(x+i\tau)\,d\tau\Big|\lesssim_{h}|y|.\qed $$

#### Proof of Proposition 9.2.

By [36, (9.5.9)], one has the functional equation

$$ \displaystyle H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(w) \displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(-2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}-it)^{2}}(-w)^{-\frac{1}{2}-it}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it,\frac{1}{2}+it;1+2it;w^{-1}\Big) \displaystyle+\frac{\Gamma(2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}+it)^{2}}(-w)^{-\frac{1}{2}+it}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it,\frac{1}{2}-it;1-2it;w^{-1}\Big)\quad\text{for }\quad w\in\mathbf{C}\setminus[0,\infty). $$

Denote

$$ \displaystyle\rho(u)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-u}}{1+\sqrt{1-u}}=\frac{u}{(1+\sqrt{1-u})^{2}}, $$

and note that

$$ \displaystyle 4w\rho(w^{-1})=\Big(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-w^{-1}}}{2}\Big)^{-2}. $$

Then by [36, (9.6.12)] and (9.16), the hypergeometrics on the right hand side of (9.14) satisfy the further functional equations

$$ \displaystyle(-w)^{-\frac{1}{2}-it}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+it,\frac{1}{2}+it;1+2it;w^{-1}\Big)=(-4\rho(w^{-1}))^{\frac{1}{2}+it}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}+it;1+it;\rho(w^{-1})^{2}\Big) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle(-w)^{-\frac{1}{2}+it}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}-it,\frac{1}{2}-it;1-2it;w^{-1}\Big)=(-4\rho(w^{-1}))^{\frac{1}{2}-it}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}-it;1-it;\rho(w^{-1})^{2}\Big), $$

again for $w\in\mathbf{C}\setminus[0,\infty)$ . Inserting these into (9.14),

$$ \displaystyle H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(w) \displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(-2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}-it)^{2}}(-4\rho(w^{-1}))^{\frac{1}{2}+it}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}+it;1+it;\rho(w^{-1})^{2}\Big) \displaystyle+\frac{\Gamma(2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}+it)^{2}}(-4\rho(w^{-1}))^{\frac{1}{2}-it}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}-it;1-it;\rho(w^{-1})^{2}\Big)\quad\text{for }\quad w\in\mathbf{C}\setminus[0,\infty). $$

Observe from (3.14) that the coefficients in the Taylor expansion of ${}_{2}F_{1}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\pm it;1\pm it;\rho)$ (as a function of $\rho$ ) at $\rho=0$ are bounded independent of $t$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\pm it;1\pm it;\rho\Big)=1+O(\rho)\qquad\text{for}\qquad|\rho|\ll 1. $$

Noting that $|\rho(w^{-1})|\lesssim|w|^{-1}$ for $|w|\gg 1$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(w)=\frac{\Gamma(-2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}-it)^{2}}(-4\rho(w^{-1}))^{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1+O(|w|^{-2}))+\frac{\Gamma(2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}+it)^{2}}(-4\rho(w^{-1}))^{\frac{1}{2}-it}(1+O(|w|^{-2})) $$

for $w\in\mathbf{C}\setminus[0,\infty)$ with $|w|\gg 1$ . Taking $w=1-z^{-2}$ with $z$ as in the statement of Proposition 9.2,

$$ \displaystyle H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2}) \displaystyle=\frac{\Gamma(-2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}-it)^{2}}\Big(-4\rho\Big(\frac{1}{1-z^{-2}}\Big)\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1+O(|z|^{4})) \displaystyle+\frac{\Gamma(2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}+it)^{2}}\Big(-4\rho\Big(\frac{1}{1-z^{-2}}\Big)\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}-it}(1+O(|z|^{4})). $$

By Stirling’s approximation,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\Gamma(-2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}-it)^{2}}4^{\frac{1}{2}+it}=\frac{e^{i\pi/4}}{\sqrt{\pi t}}(1+O(t^{-1}))\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{\Gamma(2it)}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}+it)^{2}}4^{\frac{1}{2}-it}=\frac{e^{-i\pi/4}}{\sqrt{\pi t}}(1+O(t^{-1})). $$

Thus,

$$ \displaystyle H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2}) \displaystyle=\frac{e^{i\pi/4}}{\sqrt{\pi t}}\Big(-\rho\Big(\frac{1}{1-z^{-2}}\Big)\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{4})) \displaystyle+\frac{e^{-i\pi/4}}{\sqrt{\pi t}}\Big(-\rho\Big(\frac{1}{1-z^{-2}}\Big)\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}-it}(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{4})). $$

Expanding the definition of $\rho$ and simplifying,

$$ \displaystyle-\rho\Big(\frac{1}{1-z^{-2}}\Big)=\Big(\frac{z}{1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}}}\Big)^{2}. $$

Taking logs,

$$ \displaystyle\log\Big[-\rho\Big(\frac{1}{1-z^{-2}}\Big)\Big]=2\log\Big(\frac{z}{1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}}}\Big)=2\log z-2\log(1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}}) $$

(here we are using the assumption in Proposition 9.2 that $\re z>0$ to make the first equality hold with the principal branch of $\log$ ). As in the statement of Proposition 9.2, denote

$$ \displaystyle\phi(z)=-\log(1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}}), $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\log\Big[-\rho\Big(\frac{1}{1-z^{-2}}\Big)\Big]=2(\log z+\phi(z)). $$

Writing $\zeta^{\frac{1}{2}\pm it}=\zeta^{\frac{1}{2}}\exp(\pm it\log\zeta)$ in (9.17),

$$ \displaystyle H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})=\frac{z}{1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}}} \displaystyle\Big[\frac{e^{i\pi/4}}{\sqrt{\pi t}}\exp(2it[\log z+\phi(z)])(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{4})) \displaystyle+\frac{e^{-i\pi/4}}{\sqrt{\pi t}}\exp(-2it[\log z+\phi(z)])(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{4}))\Big]. $$

By assumption in Proposition 9.2, $\im z\geq 0$ , so $\Arg z\geq 0$ . Moreover, since by assumption $|z|\ll 1$ , we have $\Arg z\gg\im z$ . Thus by Lemma 9.7,

$$ \displaystyle\im[\log z+\phi(z)]=\Arg z+O(\im z)\gtrsim\Arg z. $$

In particular, $\log z+\phi(z)$ has nonnegative imaginary part. It follows from this nonnegativity that the exponential in the first term in (9.18) has absolute value $\leq 1$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle H_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})=\frac{z}{1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}}}\Big[\frac{e^{-i\pi/4}}{\sqrt{\pi t}}\exp(-2it[\log z+\phi(z)])(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{4}))+O(t^{-\frac{1}{2}})\Big]. $$

Multiplying both sides by $t^{4k-2}e^{-\pi t}$ transforms this into an estimate for $\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})=t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}\frac{\pi^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-i\pi/4}z}{1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}}}e^{-\pi t}\exp(-2it[\log z+\phi(z)])(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{4}))+O(t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}|z|e^{-\pi t}). $$

Absorbing $e^{-\pi t}$ into the exponential,

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})=t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}\frac{\pi^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-i\pi/4}z}{1+\sqrt{1-z^{2}}}\exp(-2it[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)])(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{4}))+O(t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}|z|e^{-\pi t}). $$

This is the desired estimate (9.2). ∎

#### Corollary 9.8.

Let $\delta>0$ be arbitrarily small. Then there exists $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $\re z>0$ , such that for $t\gg 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})|\gtrsim_{\delta}e^{-\delta t}. $$

#### Proof.

Fix $0<y\ll 1$ , and let $z=x+iy$ for some $x>0$ with $x\ll_{\delta}1$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\re(2i[\log(-i(iy))+\phi(iy)])=0, $$

so by continuity, we may assume $x$ is small enough that

$$ \displaystyle\re(2i[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)])\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\delta. $$

Then from Proposition 9.2, we see that indeed

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})|\gtrsim_{\delta}e^{-\delta t} $$

for $t\gg 1$ . ∎

In the range that is relevant for us, the exponential term in (9.2) is controlled by the following lemma.

#### Lemma 9.9.

Let $z=T^{-1}+iy$ for some $y\in[0,T^{-\frac{1}{3}}]$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\re(2it[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)])\gtrsim\frac{t}{Ty+1}. $$

In particular, this real part is positive.

#### Proof.

Write

$$ \displaystyle\re(2it[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)]) \displaystyle=-2t\im\log(y-iT^{-1})-2t\im\phi(T^{-1}+iy) \displaystyle=2t\Arg(y+iT^{-1})+O(t|\im\phi(T^{-1}+iy)|). $$

We can lower bound

$$ \displaystyle\Arg(y+iT^{-1})=\Arg(Ty+i)\gtrsim\frac{1}{Ty+1}, $$

so we will be done if we can show that

$$ \displaystyle|\im\phi(T^{-1}+iy)|\ll\frac{1}{Ty+1}. $$

By inspection of the definition of $\phi$ , we can write $\phi(w)=\tilde{\phi}(w^{2})$ , where $\tilde{\phi}$ is holomorphic near $0$ and real-valued on the real line. Then

$$ \displaystyle\phi(T^{-1}+iy)=\tilde{\phi}(T^{-2}-y^{2}+2iT^{-1}y). $$

It follows from Lemma 9.7 that

$$ \displaystyle|\im\phi(T^{-1}+iy)|\lesssim T^{-1}y\ll\frac{1}{Ty+1} $$

(here the second inequality is because $T\gg 1$ and $y\in[0,T^{-\frac{1}{3}}]$ ). Thus (9.19) holds. ∎

#### Corollary 9.10.

There is a constant $c\gtrsim 1$ , such that the following holds. Let $z=T^{-1}+iy$ for some $y\in[0,T^{-\frac{1}{3}}]$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})|\lesssim t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}|z|\exp\Big(-\frac{ct}{Ty+1}\Big)\leq t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}|z|. $$

#### Proof.

Combine Proposition 9.2 and Lemma 9.9. ∎

In the critical range, the following proposition separates the smooth and oscillatory parts of the asymptotic (9.2) in Proposition 9.2 (after multiplying both sides of (9.2) by $z^{p}$ for any fixed $p\in\mathbf{R}$ ).

#### Proposition 9.11.

Assume $1<t\leq T^{\frac{2}{3}}$ . Let $p\in\mathbf{R}$ . Then there exists a smooth function $\rho$ on $[2T^{-1},T^{-\frac{1}{3}}]$ obeying the derivative bounds

$$ \displaystyle|\rho^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{p,j}y^{-j}\qquad\textnormal{for all}\qquad j\geq 0\textnormal{ and }y\in[2T^{-1},T^{-\frac{1}{3}}], $$

such that for $z=T^{-1}+iy$ with $y\in[2T^{-1},T^{-\frac{1}{3}}]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle z^{p}\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})=t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}y^{p+1}\rho(y)e^{-2it\log y}+O_{p}(t^{4k-\frac{7}{2}}y^{p+1}). $$

Explicitly, one can take

$$ \displaystyle\rho(y)=\Big(\frac{1}{Ty}+i\Big)^{p+1}\psi(z)\exp\Big(-2it\Big[\log\Big(1-\frac{i}{Ty}\Big)+\phi(z)\Big]\Big), $$

where $\phi,\psi$ are as in Proposition 9.2. To be clear, although $\rho$ depends on $p,t,T$ , the implicit constants in (9.20) are independent of $t,T$ .

#### Proof.

By Proposition 9.2,

$$ \displaystyle t^{-4k+\frac{5}{2}}z^{p}\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})=z^{p+1}\psi(z)e^{-2it[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)]}(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{4}))+O(|z|^{p+1}e^{-\pi t}). $$

By the positivity assertion in Lemma 9.9 and the fact that $|z|\sim y$ ,

$$ \displaystyle t^{-4k+\frac{5}{2}}z^{p}\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})=z^{p+1}\psi(z)e^{-2it[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)]}+O_{p}(t^{-1}y^{p+1}+y^{p+5}+y^{p+1}e^{-\pi t}). $$

Since $t\leq T^{\frac{2}{3}}$ and $y\leq T^{-\frac{1}{3}}$ , the first error term dominates the other two, so

$$ \displaystyle t^{-4k+\frac{5}{2}}z^{p}\widetilde{H}_{\frac{1}{2}+it}(1-z^{-2})=z^{p+1}\psi(z)e^{-2it[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)]}+O_{p}(t^{-1}y^{p+1}). $$

Writing $z=y(\frac{1}{Ty}+i)$ , we can express the main term on the right hand side as

$$ \displaystyle z^{p+1}\psi(z)e^{-2it[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)]}=y^{p+1}\rho(y)e^{-2it\log y}, $$

where $\rho$ is given by (9.22). Then multiplying both sides of (9.23) by $t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}$ yields (9.21).

It remains to check that $\rho$ obeys the derivative bounds in (9.20). Write

$$ \displaystyle\rho=\rho_{1}^{p+1}\rho_{2}\exp(-\rho_{3}-\rho_{4}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{1}(y)=\frac{1}{Ty}+i,\qquad\rho_{2}(y)=\psi(z),\qquad\rho_{3}(y)=2it\log\Big(1-\frac{i}{Ty}\Big),\qquad\rho_{4}(y)=2it\phi(z). $$

Trivially

$$ \displaystyle|\rho_{1}(y)|\sim 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\rho_{1}^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{j}\frac{1}{Ty^{j+1}}\lesssim y^{-j}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 1, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle|\rho_{2}^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{j}1\lesssim y^{-j}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 0. $$

Taylor expanding the logarithm in $\rho_{3}$ (which is valid because $Ty\geq 2$ ), we see that

$$ \displaystyle|\rho_{3}^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{j}\Big(\frac{t}{Ty}\Big)y^{-j}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 0. $$

Since $\phi(z)$ is a function of $z^{2}$ , we have $\phi^{\prime}(0)=0$ , so $|\phi^{\prime}(z)|\lesssim|z|\lesssim y$ . The higher derivatives are trivially bounded by $1$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle|\rho_{4}^{\prime}(y)|\lesssim ty\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\rho_{4}^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{j}t\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 2. $$

Since $t\leq T^{\frac{2}{3}}$ and $y\leq T^{-\frac{1}{3}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\rho_{4}^{\prime}(y)|\lesssim T^{\frac{1}{3}}\leq y^{-1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\rho_{4}^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{j}T^{\frac{2}{3}}\leq y^{-2}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 2. $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle|\rho_{4}^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{j}y^{-j}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 1. $$

Computing the derivatives of $\rho$ using (9.24) and the product and chain rules, and then applying (9.25), (9.26), (9.27), and (9.28),

$$ \displaystyle|\rho^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{p,j}\Big(\frac{t}{Ty}+1\Big)^{j}y^{-j}\exp(-\re[\rho_{3}(y)+\rho_{4}(y)])\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 0. $$

By Lemma 9.9 and the fact that $Ty\geq 2$ (in particular $Ty\gtrsim 1$ ),

$$ \displaystyle\re[\rho_{3}(y)+\rho_{4}(y)]=\re(2it[\log(-iy^{-1}z)+\phi(z)])=\re(2it[\log(-iz)+\phi(z)])\geq\frac{ct}{Ty} $$

for some $c\gtrsim 1$ . Inserting this into (9.29),

$$ \displaystyle|\rho^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{p,j}\Big(\frac{t}{Ty}+1\Big)^{j}y^{-j}\exp\Big(-\frac{ct}{Ty}\Big)\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 0. $$

The product of the first and third terms is $\lesssim_{j}1$ , so we conclude

$$ \displaystyle|\rho^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{p,j}y^{-j}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 0. $$

This is the desired estimate (9.20). ∎

## 10. Averaging the u-channel conformal block when $t>1$

In this section we prove Proposition 7.7. Let $s=\frac{1}{2}+it$ with $t>1$ as in the statement of the proposition.

### 10.1. The rapidly decaying range: $t\ggg T$

Suppose $t\geq T\log^{2}T$ . Then taking absolute values in the integral (5.5) defining $W(s)$ and applying Corollary 9.5 gives $|W(s)|\lesssim t^{-\infty}$ . Thus Proposition 7.7 holds in the range $t\geq T\log^{2}T$ .

### 10.2. The oscillatory range: $T\lesssim t\lessapprox T$

Now suppose $T\lesssim t\lessapprox T$ . Then to prove Proposition 7.7, we must show that

$$ \displaystyle W(s)=(1+\widetilde{O}(T^{-6\varepsilon}))\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}e^{-2t/T}\exp\Big(-\Big(\frac{t-T}{H}\Big)^{2}\Big)+\widetilde{O}(H/T). $$

For $z$ as in (5.14), Proposition 9.1 (with $M=1$ ) tells us that there exists $J\geq 0$ depending only on $\varepsilon$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{2})=\frac{t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}}{2\sqrt{\pi z}}\Big[e^{-2tz}\sum_{j=0}^{J}c_{j}(tz^{3})^{j}+O(e^{-2t\re z}|tz|^{-1}+t^{-1})\Big], $$

where the $c_{j}$ are absolute constants with $c_{0}=1$ . Noting that $e^{-2t\re z}\leq 1$ and $|z|\leq 1$ , we see that the error term is $\lesssim|tz|^{-1}$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle W(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{J}W_{j}(t)+O(E(t)), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle W_{j}(t)=\frac{c_{j}}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}Ht^{j}\int_{-T^{\varepsilon}/H}^{T^{\varepsilon}/H}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}e^{2iTy-2tz}z^{3j}\,dy $$

and

$$ \displaystyle E(t)=\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}H\int_{-T^{\varepsilon}/H}^{T^{\varepsilon}/H}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}|tz|^{-1}\,dy. $$

Since $t\lessapprox T$ , we have $(t/T)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}\lessapprox 1$ . Since $t\gtrsim T$ and $z=T^{-1}+iy$ , we also have $|tz|^{-1}\lesssim(T|y|+1)^{-1}$ . It follows that up to a log factor, the dominant contribution to $E(t)$ comes from $|y|\lesssim T^{-1}$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle E(t)\lessapprox H/T. $$

It remains to estimate $W_{j}(t)$ . We are only interested in $j\leq J$ , and $J$ depends only on $\varepsilon$ , so in the remainder of this subsection we suppress dependence of implicit constants on $j$ . Completing the integral defining $W_{j}(t)$ to an integral over $\mathbf{R}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle W_{j}(t)=\widetilde{W}_{j}(t)+O(T^{-\infty}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{j}(t)=\frac{c_{j}}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}Ht^{j}\int_{\mathbf{R}}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}e^{2iTy-2tz}z^{3j}\,dy. $$

Writing $z$ in terms of $y$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{j}(t)=\frac{c_{j}}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}Ht^{j}e^{-2t/T}\int_{\mathbf{R}}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}e^{2i(T-t)y}(T^{-1}+iy)^{3j}\,dy. $$

Rescaling $y$ by $H$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{j}(t)=\frac{c_{j}}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{j}e^{-2t/T}\int_{\mathbf{R}}e^{-y^{2}}e^{2i(T-t)H^{-1}y}(T^{-1}+iH^{-1}y)^{3j}\,dy. $$

Expanding the $3j$ th power,

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{j}(t)=\frac{c_{j}}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{j}e^{-2t/T}\sum_{\ell+m=3j}\binom{3j}{\ell}H^{-\ell}T^{-m}\int_{\mathbf{R}}(iy)^{\ell}e^{-y^{2}}e^{2i(T-t)H^{-1}y}\,dy. $$

Denote

$$ \displaystyle g(\xi)=\int_{\mathbf{R}}e^{-y^{2}}e^{i\xi y}\,dy=\sqrt{\pi}e^{-\frac{1}{4}\xi^{2}}. $$

Then we can express the above as

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{j}(t)=\frac{c_{j}}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{j}e^{-2t/T}\sum_{\ell+m=3j}\binom{3j}{\ell}H^{-\ell}T^{-m}g^{(\ell)}\Big(\frac{2(T-t)}{H}\Big). $$

If $|t-T|\geq H\log T$ , then $|\widetilde{W}_{j}(t)|\lesssim T^{-\infty}$ because of the decay of $g^{(\ell)}$ , so $|W_{j}(s)|\lesssim T^{-\infty}$ , and the desired bound (10.1) follows from (10.2) and (10.3).

Suppose instead that $|t-T|\lessapprox H$ . Explicitly differentiating $g$ gives

$$ \displaystyle|g^{(\ell)}(\xi)|\lessapprox_{\ell}g(\xi)\qquad\text{for}\qquad|\xi|\lessapprox 1. $$

Therefore

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{W}_{j}(t)| \displaystyle\lessapprox T^{j}e^{-2t/T}\sum_{\ell+m=3j}H^{-\ell}T^{-m}g\Big(\frac{2(T-t)}{H}\Big) \displaystyle\lesssim T^{j}H^{-3j}e^{-2t/T}g\Big(\frac{2(T-t)}{H}\Big) \displaystyle=T^{-6\varepsilon j}e^{-2t/T}g\Big(\frac{2(T-t)}{H}\Big). $$

When $j=0$ , we have $c_{0}=1$ , so (10.6) specializes to

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}e^{-2t/T}g\Big(\frac{2(T-t)}{H}\Big). $$

Putting (10.8) and (10.9) together,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{J}\widetilde{W}_{j}(t)=(1+\widetilde{O}(T^{-6\varepsilon}))\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}e^{-2t/T}g\Big(\frac{2(T-t)}{H}\Big). $$

Inserting (10.4) and (10.5),

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{J}W_{j}(t)=(1+\widetilde{O}(T^{-6\varepsilon}))\frac{1}{2}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}e^{-2t/T}\exp\Big(-\Big(\frac{t-T}{H}\Big)^{2}\Big)+O(T^{-\infty}). $$

Combined with (10.2) and (10.3), this implies (10.1).

### 10.3. The smooth range: $1<t\ll T$ and $|y|\ggg T^{-1}$

At this point, we have proved Proposition 7.7 whenever $t\gtrsim T$ . In this subsection, suppose $1<t\leq\frac{1}{2}T$ . In this range, the hypothesis in Proposition 9.1 that $\re z\gtrsim t^{-\frac{2}{3}+\varepsilon}|z|$ may not hold for all $z$ as in (5.14). Therefore, we cannot use Proposition 9.1. Instead, we use that because $t\leq\frac{1}{2}T$ , the function $y\mapsto\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{2})$ is smooth at scale $T^{-1}$ , and so the integral defining $W(s)$ exhibits cancellation coming from the phase $e^{2iTy}$ . We make this precise by an integration by parts argument.

Fix $\eta>0$ small. Then split

$$ \displaystyle T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}H^{-1}|W(s)| \displaystyle\leq\Big|\int_{|y|\lesssim T^{-1+\eta}}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}e^{2iTy}z^{\frac{1}{2}}\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{2})\,dy\Big| \displaystyle+\Big|\int_{T^{-1+\eta}\lesssim|y|\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}e^{2iTy}z^{\frac{1}{2}}\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{2})\,dy\Big| $$

(with a smooth cutoff at $|y|\sim T^{-1+\eta}$ ). The first integral on the right is estimated in the next subsection. In this subsection we treat the second integral: we show by integration by parts that

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{T^{-1+\eta}\lesssim|y|\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}e^{2iTy}z^{\frac{1}{2}}\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{2})\,dy\Big|\lesssim_{\eta}T^{-\infty}. $$

By the exponential decay of the Gaussian in the integrand together with the trivial bound in Proposition 9.4, the sharp cutoff to $|y|\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H=T^{-\frac{1}{3}-\varepsilon}$ can be replaced by a smooth cutoff to $|y|\lesssim T^{-\frac{1}{3}}$ . Then by dyadic decomposition, (10.11) reduces to the estimate

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{|y|\sim Y}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}e^{2iTy}z^{\frac{1}{2}}\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{2})\,dy\Big|\lesssim_{\eta}T^{-\infty} $$

for $T^{-1+\eta}\leq Y\leq T^{-\frac{1}{3}}$ .

For the remainder of this section, implicit constants may depend on $\eta$ . Let

$$ \displaystyle F(z)=z^{\frac{1}{2}}\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{2}),\qquad F_{Y}(\tilde{z})=F(Y\tilde{z}),\qquad F_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})=e^{2TY\tilde{z}}F_{Y}(\tilde{z}). $$

Then the left hand side of (10.12) is

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:u_smooth_after_dyadic}=\Big|\int_{|y|\sim Y}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}e^{2iTy}F(z)\,dy\Big|. $$

Substituting $y=Y\tilde{y}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:u_smooth_after_dyadic}=Y\Big|\int_{|\tilde{y}|\sim 1}e^{-(HY\tilde{y})^{2}}e^{2iTY\tilde{y}}F_{Y}(\tilde{z})\,d\tilde{y}\Big|, $$

where we denote

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{z}=z/Y=T^{-1}/Y+iy/Y=(TY)^{-1}+i\tilde{y}. $$

The function $\tilde{y}\mapsto e^{-(HY\tilde{y})^{2}}$ obeys uniform derivative bounds for $|\tilde{y}|\sim 1$ , i.e., the $j$ th derivative at $\tilde{y}$ is $O_{j}(1)$ for each $j\geq 0$ . Therefore, this function can be absorbed into the smooth cutoff in (10.13), giving

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:u_smooth_after_dyadic}\lesssim Y\Big|\int_{|\tilde{y}|\sim 1}e^{2iTY\tilde{y}}F_{Y}(\tilde{z})\,d\tilde{y}\Big|. $$

Since $Y\geq T^{-1+\eta}$ , we have $(TY)^{-1}\leq T^{-\eta}$ , so $|\tilde{y}|\sim 1$ if and only if $|\tilde{z}|\sim 1$ . Thus, writing the above as an integral over $\tilde{z}$ rather than $\tilde{y}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:u_smooth_after_dyadic} \displaystyle\lesssim Y\Big|\int_{(TY)^{-1}-i\infty}^{(TY)^{-1}+i\infty}\mathds{1}_{|\tilde{z}|\sim 1}e^{2TY(\tilde{z}-(TY)^{-1})}F_{Y}(\tilde{z})\,d\tilde{z}\Big| \displaystyle\lesssim Y\Big|\int_{(TY)^{-1}-i\infty}^{(TY)^{-1}+i\infty}\mathds{1}_{|\tilde{z}|\sim 1}F_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})\,d\tilde{z}\Big|. $$

For notational convenience, let $\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathbf{C}$ denote the line $\re\tilde{z}=(TY)^{-1}$ . Then the inequality above means that there exists $\chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})$ obeying uniform derivative bounds (see below) and with support contained in $\{|\tilde{z}|\sim 1\}$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:u_smooth_after_dyadic}\lesssim Y\Big|\int_{\mathcal{L}}\chi(\tilde{z})F_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})\,d\tilde{z}\Big|. $$

Here “uniform derivative bounds” means

$$ \displaystyle|\chi^{(j)}(\tilde{z})|\lesssim_{j}1\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 0\text{ and }\tilde{z}\in\mathcal{L}. $$

Thus to prove (10.12), it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{\mathcal{L}}\chi(\tilde{z})F_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})\,d\tilde{z}\Big|\lesssim T^{-\infty}. $$

The first step toward proving (10.14) is to show that $F_{Y,T}$ obeys an ODE which can be analyzed explicitly. The hypergeometric ODE is

$$ \displaystyle w(1-w)H_{s}^{\prime\prime}(w)+(1-2w)H_{s}^{\prime}(w)-\Big(\frac{1}{4}+t^{2}\Big)H_{s}(w)=0. $$

This translates to the ODE

$$ \displaystyle F^{\prime\prime}(z)-\frac{2z}{1-z^{2}}F^{\prime}(z)-\frac{\frac{1}{4}+4t^{2}-\frac{1}{4}z^{-2}}{1-z^{2}}F(z)=0 $$

for $F$ , which in turn yields the ODE

$$ \displaystyle F_{Y}^{\prime\prime}(\tilde{z})-\frac{2Y^{2}\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}F_{Y}^{\prime}(\tilde{z})-\frac{\frac{1}{4}Y^{2}+4(tY)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\tilde{z}^{-2}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}F_{Y}(\tilde{z})=0 $$

for $F_{Y}$ . In other words, $F_{Y}$ is killed by the differential operator

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{Y}=\partial_{\tilde{z}}^{2}-\frac{2Y^{2}\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}\partial_{\tilde{z}}-\frac{\frac{1}{4}Y^{2}+4(tY)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\tilde{z}^{-2}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}. $$

Let

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}=e^{2TY\tilde{z}}\circ\mathcal{P}_{Y}\circ e^{-2TY\tilde{z}},\qquad\text{so}\qquad\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}F_{Y,T}=0. $$

Expanding $\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}$ by the product rule,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}=\partial_{\tilde{z}}^{2}-\Big(\frac{2Y^{2}\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}+4TY\Big)\partial_{\tilde{z}}+4T^{2}Y^{2}+\frac{4TY^{3}\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}-\frac{\frac{1}{4}Y^{2}+4(tY)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\tilde{z}^{-2}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}. $$

The formal adjoint of $\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}$ (with respect to the symmetric pairing on $L^{2}(\mathcal{L})$ rather than the Hermitian pairing) is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*} \displaystyle=\partial_{\tilde{z}}^{2}+\partial_{\tilde{z}}\circ\Big(\frac{2Y^{2}\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}+4TY\Big)+4T^{2}Y^{2}+\frac{4TY^{3}\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}-\frac{\frac{1}{4}Y^{2}+4(tY)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\tilde{z}^{-2}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}} \displaystyle=\partial_{\tilde{z}}^{2}+\Big(\frac{2Y^{2}\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}+4TY\Big)\partial_{\tilde{z}}+\frac{2Y^{2}+2Y^{4}\tilde{z}^{2}}{(1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2})^{2}}+4T^{2}Y^{2}+\frac{4TY^{3}\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}-\frac{\frac{1}{4}Y^{2}+4(tY)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}\tilde{z}^{-2}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}. $$

Write this as

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}=\partial_{\tilde{z}}^{2}+TY\varphi_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})\partial_{\tilde{z}}+(TY)^{2}\psi_{Y,T}(\tilde{z}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})=4+\frac{2T^{-1}Y\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})=4+\frac{2T^{-2}(1+Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2})}{(1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2})^{2}}+\frac{4T^{-1}Y\tilde{z}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}-\frac{\frac{1}{4}T^{-2}+4(t/T)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(TY)^{-2}\tilde{z}^{-2}}{1-Y^{2}\tilde{z}^{2}}. $$

Recalling the inequalities $t\leq\frac{1}{2}T$ and $T^{-1+\eta}\leq Y\leq T^{-\frac{1}{3}}$ , we see that when $|\tilde{z}|\sim 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\varphi_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})|\lesssim 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\psi_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})|\lesssim 1. $$

It follows from Cauchy’s estimates for derivatives of holomorphic functions that when $|\tilde{z}|\sim 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\varphi_{Y,T}^{(j)}(\tilde{z})|\lesssim_{j}1\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\psi_{Y,T}^{(j)}(\tilde{z})|\lesssim_{j}1\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 0. $$

Observe furthermore that when $|\tilde{z}|\sim 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\psi_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})|\sim 1; $$

indeed, of the four terms in (10.16), the second and third have absolute value $\ll 1$ , and the fourth has absolute value $\leq 4(\frac{1}{2})^{2}+o(1)=1+o(1)$ because $t\leq\frac{1}{2}T$ , so the last three terms put together are still too small to cancel out the first term, which is $4$ . From (10.17) and (10.18), it follows that when $|\tilde{z}|\sim 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\Big(\frac{1}{\psi_{Y,T}}\Big)^{(j)}(\tilde{z})\Big|\lesssim_{j}1\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 0. $$

In summary, $\varphi_{Y,T}$ , $\psi_{Y,T}$ , and $1/\psi_{Y,T}$ all obey uniform derivative bounds on $\{|\tilde{z}|\sim 1\}$ .

Now, the reason we are interested in $\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}$ is that $F_{Y,T}$ is orthogonal to the image of $\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}$ acting on $C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})$ : we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{L}}\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}(g)F_{Y,T}=\int_{\mathcal{L}}g\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}F_{Y,T}=0 $$

for all $g\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})$ . Thus in (10.14), we can modify $\chi$ by any element of $\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})$ without changing the value of the integral.

#### Lemma 10.1.

Let $\chi_{0}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})$ , with support contained in $\{|\tilde{z}|\sim 1\}$ , obey the uniform derivative bounds $\|\chi_{0}^{(j)}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})}\lesssim_{j}1$ for all $j\geq 0$ . Then for any $n\geq 0$ , there exists $\chi_{n}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})$ with support contained in the support of $\chi_{0}$ , obeying the uniform derivative bounds $\|\chi_{n}^{(j)}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})}\lesssim_{j,n}1$ for all $j\geq 0$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\chi_{0}\equiv(TY)^{-n}\chi_{n}\mod\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L}). $$

This congruence condition means that there exists $g\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}g=\chi_{0}-(TY)^{-n}\chi_{n}. $$

#### Proof.

It suffices to prove this for $n=1$ , because the general case can be obtained from the $n=1$ case by iteration. Let

$$ \displaystyle g=\frac{\chi_{0}}{(TY)^{2}\psi_{Y,T}}. $$

Then define $\chi_{1}$ to make (10.19) hold with $n=1$ , so take

$$ \displaystyle\chi_{1}=TY(\chi_{0}-\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}g). $$

Clearly both $g$ and $\chi_{1}$ have support contained in that of $\chi_{0}$ . By (10.15),

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}g=\frac{1}{(TY)^{2}}\Big(\frac{\chi_{0}}{\psi_{Y,T}}\Big)^{\prime\prime}+\frac{1}{TY}\varphi_{Y,T}\Big(\frac{\chi_{0}}{\psi_{Y,T}}\Big)^{\prime}+\chi_{0}. $$

Plugging this into the definition of $\chi_{1}$ above,

$$ \displaystyle\chi_{1}=-\frac{1}{TY}\Big(\frac{\chi_{0}}{\psi_{Y,T}}\Big)^{\prime\prime}-\varphi_{Y,T}\Big(\frac{\chi_{0}}{\psi_{Y,T}}\Big)^{\prime}. $$

Since $\chi_{0}$ , $\varphi_{Y,T}$ , and $1/\psi_{Y,T}$ all obey uniform derivative bounds, so does $\chi_{1}$ (recall $TY\geq T^{\eta}\geq 1$ ). ∎

Now, let $n\geq 0$ be arbitrarily large, and apply Lemma 10.1 with $\chi_{0}=\chi$ , where $\chi$ is as in (10.14). Then we get a function $\chi_{n}\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})$ obeying derivative bounds depending only on $n$ , such that the support of $\chi_{n}$ is contained in that of $\chi$ , and such that $\chi\equiv(TY)^{-n}\chi_{n}\mod\mathcal{P}_{Y,T}^{*}C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{L})$ . Using this congruence and then the fact that $TY\geq T^{\eta}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:u_smooth_goal_2}=(TY)^{-n}\Big|\int_{\mathcal{L}}\chi_{n}(\tilde{z})F_{Y,T}(\tilde{z})\,d\tilde{z}\Big|\lesssim_{n}T^{-n\eta}\|F_{Y,T}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathcal{L}\cap\{|\tilde{z}|\sim 1\})}. $$

By Proposition 9.4, the $L^{\infty}$ norm on the right hand side is $\lesssim T^{O(1)}$ . Since $n$ was arbitrary, we conclude (10.14). Above, we reduced (10.11) to (10.14). Thus (10.11) holds, and we have accomplished our goal for this subsection.

### 10.4. The trivially bounded range: $1<t\lesssim T$ and $|y|\lessapprox T^{-1}$

Let $1<t\leq\frac{1}{2}T$ as above. In the previous subsection we showed that the second term in (10.10) is $\lesssim T^{-\infty}$ . It remains to estimate the first term, which is

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{|y|\lesssim T^{-1+\eta}}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}e^{2iTy}z^{\frac{1}{2}}\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{2})\,dy\Big|. $$

Taking the absolute values inside,

$$ \displaystyle\eqref{eqn:first_term_in_I_2_split}\lesssim T^{-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}}\int_{|y|\lesssim T^{-1+\eta}}|\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{2})|\,dy. $$

Applying Proposition 9.4,

$$ \displaystyle\eqref{eqn:first_term_in_I_2_split}\lessapprox T^{-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\eta}{2}}T^{-1+\eta}t^{4k-2}=T^{-\frac{3}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\eta}t^{4k-2}. $$

Since $t\lesssim T$ , it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\eqref{eqn:first_term_in_I_2_split}\lessapprox T^{4k-\frac{7}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\eta}. $$

Inserting this and (10.11) into (10.10), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}H^{-1}|W(s)|\lessapprox T^{4k-\frac{7}{2}+\frac{3}{2}\eta} $$

(recall that implicit constants may depend on $\eta$ ). Since $\eta$ was arbitrary, we conclude that

$$ \displaystyle|W(s)|\lessapprox H/T. $$

Since $t\leq\frac{1}{2}T$ , Proposition 7.7 follows.

We have now proved Proposition 7.7 in all cases.

### 11.1. The rapidly decaying range: $t\ggg 1$ and $y\lll\frac{t}{T}$

In this subsection and the next, suppose $t\geq\log^{3}T$ . Denote

$$ \displaystyle Y_{0}=\frac{t}{T\log^{2}T}. $$

Then split

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:half_I_4_bd}=\int_{y\lesssim Y_{0}}\mathds{1}_{y\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H}I(y)\,dy+\int_{Y_{0}\lesssim y\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H}I(y)\,dy $$

(with a smooth cutoff at $y\sim Y_{0}$ ). We will estimate the first integral in this subsection and the second integral in the next.

By Corollary 9.10,

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{-2})|\lesssim t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}|z|\exp\Big(-\frac{ct}{Ty+1}\Big), $$

where $c$ is a constant $\gtrsim 1$ . When $y\lesssim Y_{0}$ and $y\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H$ , the exponent satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\frac{t}{Ty+1}\gtrsim\max\Big\{\frac{t}{TY_{0}},\frac{t}{T^{1+\varepsilon}/H}\Big\}=\max\Big\{\log^{2}T,\frac{t}{T^{\frac{2}{3}-\varepsilon}}\Big\}. $$

It follows that for $y$ as in the first integral in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:half_I_4_split}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{-2})|\lesssim T^{-\infty}t^{-\infty}. $$

Thus the whole first integral is $O(T^{-\infty}t^{-\infty})$ , and from (11.3) we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:half_I_4_bd}=\int_{Y_{0}\lesssim y\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H}I(y)\,dy+O(T^{-\infty}t^{-\infty}). $$

### 11.2. The oscillatory range: $t\ggg 1$ and $y\gtrapprox\frac{t}{T}$

As above, suppose throughout this subsection that $t\geq\log^{3}T$ .

If $t\geq T^{\frac{2}{3}}$ , then $Y_{0}\gg T^{\varepsilon}/H$ , so the integral on the right hand side of (11.4) vanishes. It follows that (11.2) holds.

If $(T/H)\log^{3}T\leq t<T^{\frac{2}{3}}$ , then $Y_{0}\geq H^{-1}\log T$ , so $\RHS\eqref{eqn:half_I_4_oscillatory_+_error}\lesssim T^{-\infty}$ because of the Gaussian factor in (11.1) and because of Corollary 9.10. Therefore (11.2) again holds.

Thus we may assume that $t\lessapprox T/H$ . Then it suffices to show that the integral on the right hand side of (11.4) satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\int_{Y_{0}\lesssim y\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H}I(y)\,dy=\frac{1}{2}e^{-2}T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\Big(-\Big(\frac{t}{T/H}\Big)^{2}\Big)e^{i\alpha(t)}+\widetilde{O}(T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{-1}). $$

Applying Proposition 9.11 with $p=-4k+\frac{1}{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle I(y)=t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}y^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}\rho(y)e^{2i(Ty-t\log y)}+O(t^{4k-\frac{7}{2}}y^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}), $$

where $\rho$ is the smooth function (9.22) on $[2T^{-1},T^{-\frac{1}{3}}]$ obeying the derivative bounds

$$ \displaystyle|\rho^{(j)}(y)|\lesssim_{j}y^{-j}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad j\geq 0. $$

Inserting this into $\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_oscillatory_goal}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_oscillatory_goal}=t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}\int_{Y_{0}\lesssim y\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}y^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}\rho(y)e^{2i(Ty-t\log y)}\,dy+O\Big(t^{4k-\frac{7}{2}}\int_{Y_{0}\lesssim y\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H}y^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}\,dy\Big). $$

The error term is

$$ \displaystyle\lesssim t^{4k-\frac{7}{2}}Y_{0}^{-4k+\frac{5}{2}}\lessapprox t^{4k-\frac{7}{2}}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{-4k+\frac{5}{2}}=T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{-1}, $$

matching the error term in our goal (11.5).

It remains to check that the main term satisfies

$$ \displaystyle t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}\int_{Y_{0}\lesssim y\leq T^{\varepsilon}/H}e^{-(Hy)^{2}}y^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}\rho(y)e^{2i(Ty-t\log y)}\,dy \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}e^{-2}T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\Big(-\Big(\frac{t}{T/H}\Big)^{2}\Big)e^{i\alpha(t)} \displaystyle+\widetilde{O}(T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{-1}). $$

Rescaling $y$ by $T/t$ , and noting that $TY_{0}/t=\log^{-2}T$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_stat_phase_goal}=t^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}\frac{t}{T}\int_{\log^{-2}T\lesssim y\leq t^{-1}T^{1+\varepsilon}/H}e^{-(Hty/T)^{2}}(ty/T)^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}\rho(ty/T)e^{2i(ty-t\log(ty/T))}\,dy. $$

Simplifying,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_stat_phase_goal}=T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}e^{-2it\log(t/T)}\int_{\log^{-2}T\lesssim y\leq t^{-1}T^{1+\varepsilon}/H}g(y)e^{2it(y-\log y)}\,dy, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle g(y)=e^{-(Hty/T)^{2}}y^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}\rho(ty/T). $$

For $y\gtrapprox 1$ , the $j$ th derivative of the Gaussian factor in $g(y)$ is $\lessapprox_{j}1$ . It follows from this and from the derivative bounds (11.6) on $\rho$ that

$$ \displaystyle|g^{(j)}(y)|\lessapprox_{j}y^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}} $$

for all $j\geq 0$ and $y$ as in (11.8). Thus by (11.8) and stationary phase,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_stat_phase_goal}=T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}e^{-2it\log(t/T)}\Big[e^{i\pi/4}\sqrt{\pi}g(1)e^{2it}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\widetilde{O}(t^{-\frac{3}{2}})\Big], $$

where the main term in brackets comes from the stationary point $y=1$ . Expanding out,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_stat_phase_goal}=\sqrt{\pi}g(1)T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}e^{i\pi/4+2it(1-\log(t/T))}+\widetilde{O}(T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{-\frac{3}{2}}). $$

By the definitions (11.9) and (9.22) of $g$ and $\rho$ (recalling that $p=-4k+\frac{1}{2}$ in the definition of $\rho$ ),

$$ \displaystyle g(1) \displaystyle=e^{-(tH/T)^{2}}\rho(t/T) \displaystyle=\exp\Big(-\Big(\frac{t}{T/H}\Big)^{2}\Big)\Big(\frac{1}{t}+i\Big)^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}\psi(z)\exp\Big(-2it\Big[\log\Big(1-\frac{i}{t}\Big)+\phi(z)\Big]\Big), $$

where $\phi,\psi$ are as in Proposition 9.2, and where $z=T^{-1}+i\frac{t}{T}$ . Making the approximations

$$ \displaystyle\Big(\frac{1}{t}+i\Big)^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}=e^{3i\pi/4}(1+O(t^{-1})) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\psi(z)=\frac{e^{-i\pi/4}}{2\sqrt{\pi}}(1+O(|z|^{2})) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\log\Big(1-\frac{i}{t}\Big)=-\frac{i}{t}+O(t^{-2}) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\phi(z)=-\log(2)+\frac{1}{4}z^{2}+O(|z|^{4}), $$

we get

$$ \displaystyle g(1)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\exp\Big(-\Big(\frac{t}{T/H}\Big)^{2}\Big)(1+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{2}))\exp\Big(\frac{i\pi}{2}-2it\Big[-\frac{i}{t}-\log(2)+\frac{1}{4}z^{2}+O(t^{-2}+|z|^{4})\Big]\Big). $$

This simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle g(1)=\frac{e^{-2}}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\exp\Big(-\Big(\frac{t}{T/H}\Big)^{2}\Big)\exp\Big(\frac{i\pi}{2}+2it\Big[\log(2)-\frac{1}{4}z^{2}\Big]\Big)+O(t^{-1}+|z|^{2}+t|z|^{4}). $$

Since $1<t\leq T^{\frac{2}{3}}$ (the upper bound coming from $t\lessapprox T/H$ ), we have

$$ \displaystyle z^{2}=\Big(T^{-1}+i\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{2}=\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{2}(t^{-1}+i)^{2}=-\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{2}(1+O(t^{-1}))=-\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{2}+O(T^{-\frac{4}{3}})=-\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{2}+O(t^{-2}). $$

In particular,

$$ \displaystyle|z|^{2}\lesssim\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{2}+t^{-2}\leq T^{-\frac{2}{3}}+t^{-2}\lesssim t^{-1}. $$

Plugging these two estimates for $z^{2}$ into (11.11),

$$ \displaystyle g(1)=\frac{e^{-2}}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\exp\Big(-\Big(\frac{t}{T/H}\Big)^{2}\Big)\exp\Big(\frac{i\pi}{2}+2it\Big[\log(2)+\frac{1}{4}\Big(\frac{t}{T}\Big)^{2}\Big]\Big)+O(t^{-1}). $$

Inserting this into (11.10) yields

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:t_stat_phase_goal}=\frac{1}{2}e^{-2}T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\exp\Big(-\Big(\frac{t}{T/H}\Big)^{2}\Big)e^{i\alpha(t)}+\widetilde{O}(T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}t^{-\frac{3}{2}}), $$

where $\alpha(t)$ is given by (7.22). This is the desired estimate (11.7), in fact with a better error term.

Above, we reduced (11.2) to (11.7) under the assumption $t\geq\log^{3}T$ . We conclude that (11.2) holds for $t\geq\log^{3}T$ .

### 11.3. The trivially bounded range: $1<t\lessapprox 1$

It remains to prove (11.2) for $1<t<\log^{3}T$ . More generally, for $1<t\lessapprox 1$ , the error term in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:half_I_4_bd}$ dominates the main term, so (11.2) reduces to

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{0}^{T^{\varepsilon}/H}I(y)\,dy\Big|\lessapprox T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}. $$

Writing out the definition (11.1) of $I(y)$ , and using Corollary 9.10 and the fact that $t\lessapprox 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|I(y)|=e^{-(Hy)^{2}}|z|^{-4k+\frac{1}{2}}|\widetilde{H}_{s}(1-z^{-2})|\lessapprox|z|^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}, $$

so

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{0}^{T^{\varepsilon}/H}I(y)\,dy\Big|\lessapprox\int_{\mathbf{R}}|z|^{-4k+\frac{3}{2}}\,dy\lesssim T^{4k-\frac{5}{2}}, $$

as desired. Thus (11.2) holds in all cases, and the proof of Proposition 7.8 is complete.
